name: Looking back on 12 years of memories

content.title: Looking back on 12 years of memories
content.summary: Our Founding Registrar Louis Ariano shares the top moments from his career at AKU.

media.alt: Looking back on 12 years of memories

content.text: Our Founding Registrar Louis Ariano is set to retire at the end of March bringing to a close a career that has seen him spearhead significant change at the University. Ahead of his final day, he shared the top moments from his time at AKU.
What inspired you to leave Canada and join AKU?

My move with my wife, Carol, (Vice-President of Human Resources at AKU) was all very serendipitous. After our younger daughter was married, we thought that if an opportunity arose for one of us to work internationally, we would pursue this possibility. A call from a 'head hunter' asking if I would be interested in the Registrar's position at AKU came up shortly after Carol and I had had this discussion and we decided to look into it further.

And then, when we arrived for my interviews in September 2007, Carol had an opportunity to meet with President Rasul and she was invited to apply for the VP Human Resource position. It all seemed too good to be true, everything seemed to be falling into place. At that time, Karachi was not as safe as it is today and we had many naysayers advising us not to come to AKU. However, we have been very blessed during our time here and I have never for a minute regretted the decision to leave Canada and come to AKU.
What was the most unexpected cultural difference you had to adjust to?

I think that there are two things. First, from a professional point of view, I was absolutely amazed to discover that for our undergraduate Medical College and School of Nursing and Midwifery students in Karachi, the Registrar's Office automatically sent end-of-semester grades to the students' parents.  And, equally, if there was any correspondence between the University and our undergraduate students, a copy of the correspondence was sent to the parents. This was completely outside my realm of experience, we would never do that in Canada. We would only ever communicate with the student.
Second, and this came later in my AKU tenure, I realised that in Pakistan and in East Africa, I was the one with the accent and that sometimes people had difficulty understanding what I said.
How have you seen AKU grow over the past 12 years?

In addition to the ever-growing international reputation enjoyed by AKU, I have been fortunate to be a part of a team of academic and administrative professionals that has seen unprecedented growth in the offering of new academic programmes at the University:  BScM; MA (Digital Journalism); MPhil (Education); MPhil (Biological and Biomedical Sciences); Associate of Science in Dental Hygiene; MSc in Advanced Practice Nursing; MSc in Advanced Practice Midwifery; Executive Masters in Media Leadership & Innovation; Diploma in Oncology Nursing. And, with a number of new programmes on the books awaiting regulatory body approval, this list will continue to grow.
What was the biggest achievement or challenge you faced at AKU?

On joining AKU, I was charged with taking the numerous student affairs and academic administration office responsibilities across the University's five campuses and unifying those services and the distributed group of staff into a global team reporting through the Registrar's Office.
I was fortunate to work with an outstanding team in Karachi, East Africa and the UK, and I had unfettered access to the Executive Committee to bring about this change.

In particular, as part of the establishment of international standards for the Registrar's Office, I am extremely proud of two accomplishments. First, as AKU had different degree and diploma parchments presented to students in Pakistan and East Africa, and as this did not meet international standards for these legal documents, I undertook a project to standardise / unify AKU's academic legal documents by preparing a University-wide harmonised degree / diploma parchment and University transcript.

Second, prior to my arrival at AKU, student records were maintained on a number of separate academic unit-specific databases such as Microsoft Excel, Lotus 1-2-3, and even a home-made database. Again, to ensure that the University met international recordkeeping standards, I led a team of IT and Registrar's Office professionals in the implementation of the University's student information system, AKUROSS, which was completed on-time and significantly under budget.
You were a part of academic leadership and engaged in day-to-day operations, how did you manage your work-life balance?

Not very well. I am very bad at ignoring the email notifications on my mobile/iPad/laptop and thus I seemed to be 'on' all the time. As someone once said of these 'conveniences': "Let me show you how to turn them off". However, I did find time to enjoy the company of AKU friends and colleagues at social events, in particular the fantastic gastronomic scene now available in Karachi.
What was your most memorable moment at AKU?

There many wonderful memories from my time at AKU such as meetings and interactions with so many smart and dedicated individuals; the opportunity to travel to northern Pakistan; receiving an Award of Distinction; but there is one memory that I will cherish forever.

The 2015 Convocations in East Africa was an intense set of three ceremonies, held over seven days, at which the Chancellor was present. During the final ceremony in Kenya, we were just about ready to go into the hall and I was giving last minute instructions to everyone - the Chancellor, President, Provost, Deans - who would be marching in the Procession. I said: "OK, we're ready, even a little bit early, but I think we should line up and head out." The Chancellor got this impish look on his face and said, "Yes, I think we should go out early, too. You know how long it takes for the deans to walk in." At which point he mimed a laboured-type of movement using a folding walker. Of course, everyone in the room burst out laughing. For me, it was an absolutely wonderful moment, which I think speaks so highly of our Chancellor's spirit, humour and goodwill. It's one of my favourite memories of AKU.
What are your plans after returning to Canada?

After living and working in Pakistan, East Africa and UK for the past 12 years, returning to Canada is not guaranteed: it's just too darn cold for too much of the year in Canada.  At present, we will begin what Carol is calling our "Gap Year", an opportunity to defuse, see what it's like not to work and think about what we'd like to do in the future. However, regardless of any of that, plans include spending time with our two granddaughters, our daughters, and my mom.
How would you describe your journey at AKU?
Incredibly satisfying!
